newsitem.title: CANADA: Market not expecting higher bid for Viridian.
newsitem.headline: Market not expecting higher bid for Viridian.

text.p: With Viridian Inc shares trading below Agrium Inc's stock swap bid value, investors on Monday did not appear to be expecting a competing offer for the fertilizer firm, analysts said.

"If you look at the stock price reaction, it's trading...pretty much on the terms, so the market is not necessarily saying that it expects a higher offer at this point in time," said CIBC Woody Gundy analyst David Davidson.
Viridian, which said on Sunday it agreed to a friendly C$1.33 billion merger with Agrium, was up 1.25 to 17.75 in midday trade in Toronto.
Agrium shares, which under the deal would be swapped on a 0.975-for-one basis, were trading at 18.40, or C$0.19 above Viridian when the exchange was factored in.
The companies also said that the deal included a C$30 million break fee that would be paid to Agrium if another suitor outbid it.

But competing North American companies that would benefit from gaining a larger piece of the continent's nitrogen-based fertilizer business would undoubtedly put the deal under their microscopes, Davidson said.

"Most other players in the fertilizer industry will obviously be dusting off their old files on Viridian to have a look at it and see if the price makes sense or if they could do something else," he said.
When Sherritt Inc was split in two last year, chairman Ian Delaney said the move was not to position the fertilizer arm for a sale, despite analyst speculation to the contrary.
Viridian subsequently made itself into an even purer fertilizer company in 1996 by spinning off its Westaim specialty products division and its Canadian oil and gas arm.

Davidson said that, given the company's previous moves, he was not surprised that Viridian was part of a deal. "In the past there have been assets up (for sale) and Agrium has maybe not been that aggressive, so maybe they were just biding their time."
Viridian shareholders will vote on the merger terms at a special meeting to be called before the end of the year, the companies said.
The merger would create one of North America's largest integrated fertilizer production and marketing operations.
The merger, which meant a combining of low-cost production and marketing assets in western Canada, Idaho, Nebraska, Texas, California and Argentina, was viewed as positive.

"There's lots of room for speculation on synergies there because of their geographical presence and obviously their facility to access cheap Canadian gas at this point in time," Davidson said. "It makes for a very good company going forward."
Natural gas is a feedstock in nitrogen-based fertilizer production.
Apart from nitrogen fertilizer, the merged firm's phosphate production would make it the leading supplier to the western North American market.
Agrium is already the third largest North American potash producer and the second largest independent retailer of agricultural crop products production services.
The deal is the latest in a string of huge North American fertilizer mergers over the past two years.
